newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-East and west German jobs gap widening.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-East and west German jobs gap widening.

text.p: Germany's Federal Labour Office said on Wednesday that the number of people out of work last month rose in seasonally-adjusted terms, and new data showed a widening gap between east and west Germany.

As companies in western Germany wrap up restructuring programmes and the economy begins to brighten, jobs are finally being created in an economic recovery that has been largely marked by rising unemployment.

But this is not the case in east Germany, where a building sector slump has followed the surge in construction activity after German unification in 1990 and is now one of the major reasons why jobless numbers continue rising in the region.
"In the jobs market, growth is divergent," Bernhard Jagoda, president of the Labour Office told a news briefing. "There is an increasing discrepancy between west and east German states."
The number of unemployed in Germany rose by 17,000 in July to 4.396 million on a seasonally-adjusted basis, causing the unemployment rate to rise slightly to 11.5 percent.
West German jobless numbers fell 10,000 to 3.029 million, or 9.8 percent, in July. The number of people out of work in east Germany rose 27,000 to 1.367 million, or 18.2 percent.
On an unadjusted basis, a politically sensitive figure but less important to financial markets, 4.354 million Germans were out of work in July, or 11.4 percent, up from 4.222 million.

The rise in unemployment in July was higher than expected by independent economists and largely attributed to sharp rises in eastern Germany, still struggling to adjust to western markets after decades of communism.
While the western German recovery is being driven by robust exports, east German businesses have not benefitted from the trend, said Jagoda, adding that domestic demand remained weak.

"The problem with eastern Germany is that too much of what is produced there is not exported," he said. "As always in July, unemployment grew for seasonal reasons. However this year the increase was stronger than usual."

Despite the fresh rise in unemployment, Jagoda saw no reason to change his forecast that the number of people out of work would average 4.3 million this year and that the situation could improve next year.
"We hope that for 1998 we will have an average jobless figure of four million or less," he said.

Economists pointed out that a mix of structural problems in the east and the weakness of the building sector were driving unemployment there and warned that the failure of government tax reform plans could have a negative impact on jobs.
While some economists saw a "turning point" reached because of the fall in west German unemployment, others were less sure.

"This is much weaker than originally expected. The east German construction sector is suffering a lot, though the west German economy is gaining a little momentum," said Guenter Redeker of Chase Investment Bank in London.
"To call this a turning point is a heroic statement. The failure of the tax reform process will be a big negative for investment."
Opposition politicians said government spending cuts and high supplementary wage costs were strangling domestic spending.
Ottmar Schreiner, financial affairs spokesman for the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), said that any tax reform must improve spending power for the broad population.
"These numbers prove the necessity of a new policy," he said. "The SPD wants a tax reform aimed at jobs, one that strengthens consumption-oriented income."
